title: Chapter 29
paragraphs: "Finally, it's over, thank God!" was Anna Arkadyevna's first thought once she'd said her last goodbye to her brother, who'd stood blocking the carriage entrance until the third bell rang. She sat down on her seat beside Annushka and looked around at the dim twilight of the sleeping car. "Thank God! Tomorrow I'll see Seryozha and Alexey Alexandrovitch, and my life will go back to normal, all nice and the same as always."

She'd been anxious all day, and that same restlessness stayed with her as she settled in for the journey, taking great care over every detail. Her small, deft hands opened and closed her little red bag, pulled out a cushion, set it on her lap, and wrapped her feet snugly before she made herself comfortable. An invalid lady nearby had already lain down to sleep. Two other women struck up a conversation with Anna, and a heavyset older lady tucked her feet under her and complained about how the train was heated. Anna answered with a few words, but seeing no real entertainment in the conversation, she asked Annushka to fetch her a lamp, hung it on the arm of her seat, and took a paper-knife and an English novel from her bag. At first she couldn't get into her reading. The commotion around her was distracting; then, once the train got moving, she found herself listening to its noises; then it was the snow beating against the left-hand window and sticking to the glass, the sight of the bundled-up guard walking past, covered in snow on one side, and the talk around her about the terrible blizzard outside — all of it pulled her attention away. Farther on, it was the same thing over and over: the same jolting and rattling, the same snow on the window, the same quick swings from stifling heat to cold and back to heat again, the same passing glimpses of the same shapes in the half-light, the same voices — and Anna finally began to read and actually take in what she was reading. Annushka was already dozing, the red bag in her lap held by her broad, gloved hands, one glove torn. Anna Arkadyevna read and understood what she read, but she found it distasteful — following the reflected lives of other people. She wanted too badly to live her own life. If she read that the novel's heroine was nursing a sick man, she wanted to be the one moving quietly around a sickroom herself; if she read about a member of Parliament giving a speech, she wanted to be the one giving it; if she read about how Lady Mary had ridden to hounds, provoked her sister-in-law, and shocked everyone with her nerve, she too wished she were doing the same. But there was nothing to actually do, so she kept twisting the smooth paper-knife in her hands and forced herself to read.

The novel's hero was already nearly at his English version of happiness — a baronetcy and an estate — and Anna felt a wish to go there with him, when she suddenly sensed that _he_ ought to feel ashamed, and that she was ashamed of the very same thing. But what did he have to be ashamed of? "What do I have to be ashamed of?" she asked herself, stung and surprised. She set the book down and sank back against the chair, gripping the paper-cutter tightly in both hands. There was nothing. She went back through all her memories of Moscow. They were all good, pleasant ones. She remembered the ball, remembered Vronsky's face full of slavish adoration, remembered everything about how she'd behaved with him — none of it was shameful. And yet, at that very point in her memories, the feeling of shame grew sharper, as though some inner voice, right when she thought of Vronsky, were telling her, "Warm, very warm, hot." "Well, what is it, then?" she said to herself firmly, shifting her position on the seat. "What does it mean? Am I afraid to look it straight in the face? What is it, really? Is it possible that something exists — or could ever exist — between me and this boy of an officer, beyond the ordinary relations one has with any acquaintance?" She laughed contemptuously and picked her book back up, but now she genuinely couldn't follow what she was reading. She ran the paper-knife along the windowpane, then pressed its smooth, cool surface to her cheek, and almost laughed out loud at the wave of delight that suddenly came over her for no reason at all. She felt as if her nerves were strings being wound tighter and tighter on some kind of screw peg. Her eyes felt like they were opening wider and wider, her fingers and toes twitched nervously, something inside her chest pressed down on her breathing, and in the uncertain half-light every shape and sound struck her with unusual vividness. Moments of doubt kept coming over her — she'd lose track of whether the train was moving forward, moving backward, or standing still altogether; whether it was Annushka beside her or a stranger. "What's that on the arm of the chair — a fur cloak, or some animal? And what am I myself? Am I myself, or some other woman?" She was afraid of giving in to this half-delirious state. But something pulled her toward it, and she could choose to yield to it or resist it. She got up to shake herself out of it, and slipped off her plaid wrap and the cape of her warm dress. For a moment she came back to herself and realized that the thin peasant who'd just come in, wearing a long overcoat with buttons missing, was the stove-tender, that he was checking the thermometer, that it was the wind and snow blowing in behind him through the door — but then everything blurred again... That long-waisted peasant seemed to be gnawing at something on the wall; the old lady began stretching her legs the whole length of the carriage, filling it with a black cloud; then came a terrible shrieking and banging, as if someone were being torn apart; then a blinding flash of red fire before her eyes, and a wall seemed to rise up and hide everything. Anna felt as though she were sinking down. But it wasn't frightening — it was delightful. A man's voice, muffled and covered in snow, shouted something close to her ear. She sat up and pulled herself together; she realized they'd reached a station, and that this was the guard. She asked Annushka to hand her the cape she'd taken off, along with her shawl, put them on, and moved toward the door.
"Do you want to get off?" asked Annushka.
"Yes, I want some air. It's so hot in here." And she opened the door. The driving snow and wind rushed at her, fighting her for control of the door. But she found she was enjoying the struggle.

She pushed the door open and went out. The wind seemed to have been lying in wait for her; with a gleeful whistle it tried to snatch her up and carry her off, but she clung to the cold doorpost and, holding her skirt, made her way down onto the platform and into the shelter of the cars. The wind had been fierce on the steps, but here on the platform, sheltered by the carriages, it had died down. With real pleasure she breathed in deep lungfuls of the freezing, snow-scented air, and, standing near the carriage, took in the platform and the lit-up station around her.
